summary:
Apollo Harness is a web app that shows, for any landing site on the Moon, how much sunlight it gets, when the Sun and Earth will set behind the surrounding terrain, and how a launch delay changes both. Mission planners, educators and the public can explore 15 CLPS and historical landing sites on a 3D Moon, click any point to analyse it live, and compare two sites or two launch dates side by side. Simple mode turns the geometry into plain countdowns ("sunrise in 37 minutes"); Scientific mode shows the angles, terrain horizons and vectors behind them.

Everything is computed from NASA data: JPL NAIF SPICE ephemeris for Sun and Earth positions, LRO LOLA terrain for 360-degree horizons, and NASA's map of permanently shadowed regions. We checked the engine against JPL Horizons (within 0.006 degrees at 13 sites) and against NASA's illumination and Earth-visibility maps (R² 0.951 and 0.953).

The challenge asks for an intuitive way to evaluate Sun and Earth visibility at candidate landing sites. Apollo Harness answers in seconds: for example, a 72-hour launch slip cuts sunlight at IM-2 Athena's site from 98.2% to 77.2% over 14 days.
details:
What it does

Apollo Harness answers the questions a lunar landing team asks first: will the site see the Sun, can it talk to Earth, and for how long? For any site on the Moon it computes sunlight and Earth line of sight over a 29.5-day lunar day, counts down to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise against the real terrain horizon, and shows how those change if the launch moves.

How it works

  • A Python engine uses NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels to place the Sun and Earth in the sky of a lunar site, and LRO LOLA elevation models (NASA GSFC PGDA product 90 for 80–90°S at 80 m per pixel, NASA PDS LDEM_64 everywhere else) to trace the 360-degree terrain horizon.
  • Precomputed 29.5-day tracks for catalog missions ship with the website, so it works offline. A live FastAPI service computes any clicked point or launch-date comparison on demand.
  • The React + CesiumJS front end draws the Moon (NASA Moon Trek LRO WAC mosaic), the mission fleet, Earth and the Sun along their true directions, and an Earth link beam that turns red when terrain hides Earth.

Features

  • 15 missions from a primary-sourced catalog: CLPS landers plus Apollo 11 and 17, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e 4 and SLIM as reference landings.
  • Simple mode (countdowns for classrooms and the public) and Scientific mode (azimuth and elevation, horizon margins, visible fraction of the Sun and Earth discs, Moon-frame vectors).
  • A 29.5-day timeline, click-anywhere or typed-coordinate analysis, and comparison of two sites or two launch dates.
  • Data provenance for every value. Missing data is shown as "Unavailable", never as zero.

Benefits and impact

Planners can test a launch window before committing to it. Educators get real NASA data as countdowns students can read. Anyone can check any point on the Moon in seconds. As commercial landers head for the lunar poles, every team has to answer these questions; for example, a 72-hour slip cuts sunlight at IM-2 Athena's site from 98.2% to 77.2% over 14 days.

Validation

  • JPL Horizons cross-check: Sun direction within 0.006° at 13 lunar sites, and 100% agreement on whether the Sun and Earth are above or below a smooth horizon.
  • NASA PGDA product 69 maps: sunlight R² 0.951 (mean error 1.45 percentage points on 305 held-out points) and Earth visibility R² 0.953 (mean error 1.40 points).

Tools and technologies

Python (SpiceyPy, rasterio, GeoPandas, NumPy), FastAPI in Docker on Render, React + TypeScript + Vite + CesiumJS on Firebase Hosting, and GitHub Actions for tests and deployment. Source code: https://github.com/k-shopnil/apolloharness

What makes it creative

The app opens like a launch: a countdown lobby and a "Takeoff with us" button. One engine reads two ways: at IM-2 Athena's site, Simple mode says "sunrise in 37 minutes", while Scientific mode shows why, with the Sun 0.08° below the terrain horizon.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty first: only published landing coordinates are shown as landing points, unknown values are never shown as zero, and the terrain model behind each result is always labelled. Earth contact is geometric line of sight only (no link budget), and the slope shown is regional terrain, not lander footing safety. We also kept the app usable offline and the live engine within a free 512 MB server.

Use of AI (SI)

We used Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code) as an AI assistant for coding and debugging, documentation, data-pipeline tooling and checks, and the design of our demo slides. All science values come from NASA data through our engine, which we validated against NASA and JPL references.
dataRefs: NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE generic kernels (Sun, Earth and Moon ephemeris)
NASA GSFC PGDA product 90: LRO LOLA south polar DEM (80 m) and permanently shadowed regions
NASA GSFC PGDA product 69: LOLA lunar illumination and Earth-visibility maps
NASA PDS Geosciences Node: LRO LOLA global DEM (LDEM_64)
NASA Moon Trek: LRO WAC global mosaic (globe imagery)
LRO Camera (LROC): landing-site imagery and coordinates
NASA Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) mission information
NASA Artemis III candidate landing regions
NASA PDS: IM-2 Athena (CLPS PRIME-1) mission context
NASA NSSDCA: Apollo landing site coordinates
NASA CCMC DONKI space weather database (via api.nasa.gov)
projectRefs: USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (IAU crater names)
Chinese Academy of Sciences: Chang'e 4 landing (reference site)
SpiceyPy: Python wrapper for NAIF SPICE (open source)
Anthropic Claude Code: AI assistant used for coding, docs and slides
